title: Formulating directional hypothesis test for a population proportion
scenario_markdown:
A consumer packaged goods company is evaluating a new ergonomic bottle design for its flagship fruit juice line. Historically, market benchmark studies established that $40\%$ ($p_0 = 0.40$) of consumers preferred the brand's packaging over top competitors.

The commercial executive team states: *'We will only invest $2.5 million to retool our bottling lines if consumer research demonstrates that more than 40% of consumers prefer this new packaging.'* A market research agency conducts a blind taste-and-handling study with $n = 500$ consumers. Formulate the statistical hypotheses, identify the tail direction, and establish the decision rule.

parameters.objective: Formulate one-tailed null and alternative hypotheses for a population proportion based on a directional business claim

assumptions: Executive investment threshold requires proving that p > 0.40
The research claim 'more than 40%' carries the burden of proof and belongs in the alternative hypothesis H1

approval.notes: Reviewed conceptual alignment: Benchmark p0 = 0.40. Directional claim 'more than 40%' defines right-tailed alternative H1: p > 0.40 vs null H0: p <= 0.40 (or p = 0.40). Clarifies that hypotheses are formulated about population parameter p, not sample statistic p_hat.

stages.prompt_markdown: Which pair of hypotheses correctly formulates the company's decision problem?

options.hint_markdown: The research claim is that preference is *greater than* $40\%$, which corresponds to an upper (right) tail test, not a lower tail.
Management will only invest if preference has increased above $40\%$; a two-tailed test would improperly trigger on a decrease in preference.

stages.explanation_markdown: The investment decision is directional: management requires proof that the proportion exceeds $40\%$. The research claim that carries the burden of proof is placed in the alternative hypothesis: $H_1: p > 0.40$. The null hypothesis represents the status quo that the new bottle does not increase preference: $H_0: p \le 0.40$ (or $H_0: p = 0.40$).

stages.prompt_markdown: Where is the rejection region located for this test, and what type of sample results provide evidence to reject $H_0$?

options.text_markdown: **Right (upper) tail**: Rejection occurs only when the sample proportion $\hat{p}$ is substantially larger than $0.40$, yielding a large positive standardized test statistic $Z > Z_\alpha$.
**Left (lower) tail**: Rejection occurs when the sample proportion is substantially smaller than $0.40$, yielding a large negative $Z < -Z_\alpha$.
options.hint_markdown: Values below $0.40$ support the null hypothesis ($p \le 0.40$); only values above $0.40$ provide evidence for $H_1: p > 0.40$.

options.text_markdown: **Center of the distribution**: Rejection occurs whenever the sample proportion is close to $0.40$.
options.hint_markdown: The center of the distribution corresponds to the null value where $H_0$ is retained.

stages.explanation_markdown: Because the inequality in the alternative hypothesis points to the right ($p > 0.40$), this is an **upper (right-tailed) test**. All of the significance level $\alpha$ is placed in the right tail. Only sample proportions $\hat{p}$ substantially greater than $0.40$ produce a test statistic $Z = \frac{\hat{p} - 0.40}{\sqrt{0.40(0.60)/n}} > Z_\alpha$ that justifies rejecting $H_0$.

stages.prompt_markdown: Why would writing the hypotheses as *'$H_0: \hat{p} = 0.40$ vs. $H_1: \hat{p} > 0.40$'* be a fundamental statistical error?

options.text_markdown: **Hypotheses are statements about unknown population parameters, not sample statistics**: $\hat{p}$ is a known sample value computed directly from the data, whereas hypothesis testing evaluates the unknown population parameter $p$.
**$\hat{p}$ is the symbol for sample variance, not proportion**: One cannot test variance using a proportion test.
options.hint_markdown: $\hat{p}$ is the sample proportion; hypotheses must be written about the population parameter $p$.

options.text_markdown: **It is not an error**: Modern statistics treats $p$ and $\hat{p}$ as completely interchangeable.
options.hint_markdown: Conflating sample statistics with population parameters is a major conceptual error in inferential statistics.

stages.explanation_markdown: A core foundation of statistical inference is that **hypotheses are always formulated about population parameters** ($p$ or $\mu$), never about sample statistics ($\hat{p}$ or $\bar{x}$). We do not hypothesize about $\hat{p}$ because we observe it directly without uncertainty. Hypothesis tests use the known sample statistic $\hat{p}$ to make an inference about the unknown population parameter $p$.
